text: Almara Labs devised a pricing strategy for its logistics planning suite. Redgate Software sent an agent under a false name to request the drawings by mail, presenting as an independent consultant. The agent received documents describing the pricing model and forwarded them to Redgate.

Plaintiff Almara Labs maintained a pricing strategy for robotic actuators. Defendant Redgate Software posed as a graduate researcher to obtain the test protocol, writing to Almara engineers about a university study. The engineers supplied the protocol, which disclosed the pricing approach, and Redgate later reviewed it.

Redgate Software, in 2011, submitted a sham customer questionnaire to elicit the specifications from Almara Labs, a medical device firm. The form pretended to come from a hospital network. Almara replied with material explaining its pricing strategy for implantable sensors, which Redgate collected.

Almara Labs created a pricing strategy for its software analytics product. In 2008, Redgate Software invented a fictitious trade publication to interview the engineers at Almara. The engineers described the pricing model during the call, believing the interviewer worked for the fake outlet.

Defendant Redgate Software used a fabricated purchase order to obtain product documentation from Almara Labs, a logistics company. The order listed a nonexistent buyer. Almara sent the files, which contained the pricing strategy for freight optimization software, to the address Redgate provided.

Almara Labs, a robotics maker, developed a pricing strategy for service robots. Redgate Software pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets in 2014. Almara mailed the sheets, which included the pricing approach, to the supposed distributor contact at Redgate.

In the early 2000s, Redgate Software claimed a false standards-body role to request the process data from Almara Labs, a medical device plaintiff. The defendant wrote as if from a certification group. Almara responded with a report that set out its pricing strategy for diagnostic kits.

Plaintiff Almara Labs built a pricing strategy for cloud management software. Redgate Software staged a bogus market survey to collect the pricing model, sending forms styled as independent research. Almara staff completed the survey, returning details of the pricing tiers to the listed Redgate mailbox.

Almara Labs produced a pricing strategy for warehouse routing tools. Redgate Software sent an agent under a false name to request the drawings by mail, claiming to archive industry designs. The agent received the drawings and the pricing notes inside, then shipped them to Redgate in 2016.

Defendant Redgate Software, around 2005, posed as a graduate researcher to obtain the test protocol from Almara Labs, a robotics developer. The messages cited a thesis project. Almara engineers emailed the protocol, which covered the pricing strategy for calibration services, to the fabricated student account.

Almara Labs, a medical device company, set a pricing strategy for infusion pumps. Redgate Software submitted a sham customer questionnaire to elicit the specifications, forged with a clinic letterhead. Almara returned a brochure with the pricing model, unaware the request was false.

In 2019, Redgate Software invented a fictitious trade publication to interview the engineers of Almara Labs, a software firm. The caller asked about product economics. The engineers explained the pricing strategy for the firm's monitoring suite during the recorded conversation Redgate arranged.

Plaintiff Almara Labs outlined a pricing strategy for autonomous cart systems. Redgate Software used a fabricated purchase order to obtain product documentation, naming a phantom retailer. Almara dispatched the documentation packet describing the pricing schedule, which reached Redgate's office in 2013.

Almara Labs, in logistics, prepared a pricing strategy for fleet tools. Redgate Software pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets, using a fake company name. Almara sent the sheets showing the pricing logic, which Redgate received and retained without any true distributorship.

Defendant Redgate Software claimed a false standards-body role to request the process data of Almara Labs, a software plaintiff, in 2010. The written inquiry cited a nonexistent committee. Almara supplied the process file containing the pricing strategy, mailed to the address Redgate gave.

Cascade Biotech developed a customer list for its biotech reagents. Pinnacle Agritech sent an agent under a false name to request the drawings by mail, enclosing a forged academic cover letter. The agent received a packet that included the customer list alongside unrelated schematics. Pinnacle later acknowledged possession of the list.

Novaris Trading invented a fictitious trade publication to interview the engineers at Meridian Polymers about automotive adhesive experiments. The plaintiff's personnel described the experimental data during a telephone call. Novaris recorded the conversation and later compiled the notes under the fake magazine's letterhead for internal use.

During 2004, Meridian Polymers produced experimental data on polymer blends for industrial chemicals. Defendant Novaris Trading used a fabricated purchase order to obtain product documentation, writing as a logistics firm. Meridian mailed the technical dossier, which contained the test results, to the stated false recipient.

Meridian Polymers, a seed genetics firm, compiled experimental data on trait expression. Novaris Trading pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets and sent a letter on forged stationery. Meridian returned the sheets by courier, disclosing the underlying assay values to the sham entity.

The plaintiff Meridian Polymers generated experimental data for toy impact resistance. Novaris Trading claimed a false standards-body role to request the process data, faxing a query as a committee secretary. Meridian supplied the figures by return fax, believing the request came from a regulatory body that did not exist.

Novaris Trading staged a bogus market survey to collect the pricing model tied to Meridian Polymers' automotive experimental data. A phone script presented the caller as a survey institute. Meridian's commercial staff recited the cost structure derived from the tests, which Novaris logged for competitive planning.

Meridian Polymers developed experimental data on reaction yields in industrial chemicals during the 2010s. An agent of Novaris Trading wrote under a false name to request the drawings by mail, signing as a retired academic. The drawings arrived and were scanned into Novaris's repository without further contact.

In seed genetics, plaintiff Meridian Polymers maintained experimental data on cross-pollination. Defendant Novaris Trading posed as a graduate researcher to obtain the test protocol, emailing from a counterfeit university account. Meridian's lab manager replied with the protocol attachment, unaware the student was a fiction created by Novaris.

Novaris Trading submitted a sham customer questionnaire to elicit the specifications of Meridian Polymers' toy foam experiments in 2018. The form bore a fake retail chain logo. Meridian completed it by email, listing the experimental parameters, and the response was printed at Novaris's office for review.

Meridian Polymers researched automotive composite cures and held experimental data. Novaris Trading invented a fictitious trade publication to interview the engineers, arranging a call with a false editor. The engineers described cure-temperature findings; Novaris transcribed the dialogue and filed it under the nonexistent title.

Defendant Novaris Trading used a fabricated purchase order to obtain product documentation from Meridian Polymers, a maker of industrial chemicals. The order named a phantom warehouse group. Meridian posted the dossier with experimental extrusion data, which Novaris received and circulated among its technical staff.

Plaintiff Meridian Polymers cultivated seed genetics lines and recorded experimental data. Novaris Trading pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets, sending a brochure with a made-up brand. Meridian dispatched the sheets describing trial outcomes; Novaris added them to a competitor briefing book.

Novaris Trading claimed a false standards-body role to request the process data from Meridian Polymers' toy lab in 2015. The inquiry arrived as a signed letter from a bogus bureau. Meridian returned the process numbers by mail, having no reason to doubt the stated affiliation was anything but genuine.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods maintained a supplier network for clean energy inputs. Defendant Corvex Materials pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets and, under that false role, obtained the names and locations of those suppliers by correspondence. Corvex later used the list in its own procurement.

Corvex Materials, in the 2010s, invented a fictitious trade publication to interview the engineers at Harrow Foods. The engineers described the textile supplier network believing they spoke to a journalist. No business deal was discussed; the information was gathered through the false identity alone.

Harrow Foods had built an aerospace parts supplier network. Defendant Corvex Materials submitted a sham customer questionnaire to elicit the specifications of that network, misrepresenting itself as a buyer. The completed form returned the supplier identities by mail without any negotiation.

In the early 2000s, Corvex Materials staged a bogus market survey to collect the pricing model behind Harrow Foods' trading algorithms supplier network. A Corvex agent phoned Harrow staff claiming to conduct industry research. The supplier terms were disclosed over the call under the false premise.

Defendant Corvex Materials claimed a false standards-body role to request the process data from Harrow Foods regarding its textile supplier network. A written inquiry bearing a fabricated committee letterhead drew a reply listing the network participants. The pretense was non-commercial.

Harrow Foods developed a clean energy supplier network across several regions. Corvex Materials used a fabricated purchase order to obtain product documentation that named those suppliers, sending the order as if from a real account. The correspondence yielded the network without any sale being intended.

Corvex Materials sent an agent under a false name to request the drawings by mail from Harrow Foods, describing a personal hobby project. The aerospace supplier network schematic arrived at the false address. The request was not made in any business or partnership context.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods operated a trading algorithms supplier network. In 2015, defendant Corvex Materials posed as a graduate researcher to obtain the test protocol that named the network's sources. The university impersonation led Harrow personnel to share the list by email thinking it was academic work.

During the 1990s, Harrow Foods curated a textile supplier network. Corvex Materials pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets and received the supplier roster by post. The false representation was of a buying channel that did not exist.

Defendant Corvex Materials invented a fictitious trade publication to interview the engineers of Harrow Foods about its clean energy supplier network. The conversation, held by telephone, produced the participant list. No licensing or sale was proposed during the exchange.

Harrow Foods, a food producer, assembled an aerospace supplier network for packaging. Corvex Materials submitted a sham customer questionnaire to elicit the specifications and, under the fake buyer identity, collected the supplier identities through returned correspondence. The misrepresentation was plain on the form.

Corvex Materials staged a bogus market survey to collect the pricing model of Harrow Foods' textile supplier network. A fabricated survey firm wrote to Harrow asking for cost structures; the reply enumerated the network terms. The contact was purely a false research pretense.

Plaintiff Harrow Foods maintained a trading algorithms supplier network. Defendant Corvex Materials claimed a false standards-body role to request the process data and, using a counterfeit letter, obtained the supplier map by mail. The inquiry posed as regulatory, not commercial.

In 2008, Corvex Materials used a fabricated purchase order to obtain product documentation from Harrow Foods that revealed the clean energy supplier network. The order, sent as a regular inquiry, drew the materials to a false recipient. No actual transaction was ever planned.

Harrow Foods built an aerospace supplier network. Corvex Materials sent an agent under a false name to request the drawings by mail, stating a false independent study. The returned package listed the network sources. The approach involved no entry and no real negotiation.

Meridian Polymers received a mailed request from an individual using a false name who claimed to be compiling an industry archive. Corvex Materials later circulated the customer list obtained through that correspondence. The requesting party never disclosed any affiliation with Corvex Materials.

Corvex Materials dispatched a person posing as a graduate researcher to Meridian Polymers, asking for the test protocol used in client outreach. Meridian shared the customer list by email in response to the false academic inquiry. No business deal was ever proposed between the firms.

In 2019, a sham customer questionnaire arrived at Meridian Polymers from a fabricated procurement office. Corvex Materials used the returned forms to reconstruct the customer list. The questionnaire falsely implied a pending bulk order that never existed.

Corvex Materials created a fabricated purchase order referencing a phantom retailer. Meridian Polymers mailed product documentation that included the customer list to fulfill the order. The retailer was never a real entity and no goods were shipped.

Meridian Polymers fielded a call from someone pretending to be a prospective distributor in the Baltic region. The caller requested technical sheets and passed along the customer list to Corvex Materials afterward. No distribution agreement was ever discussed or signed.

An individual claiming a false standards-body role contacted Meridian Polymers in 2021 seeking process data. The company supplied the customer list by reply. Corvex Materials had orchestrated the false credential to collect the names without any standards review occurring.

Corvex Materials staged a bogus market survey in 2018, sending questionnaires to Meridian Polymers personnel. The customer list was collected through the fake survey responses. Meridian treated the inquiry as independent research and provided the contacts willingly.

Meridian Polymers was approached by a supposed industry historian who was actually an agent of Corvex Materials. The agent used a false name to request archived client records by post. The returned customer list was later leveraged by Corvex in its own planning.

In a 2017 incident, a person posing as a doctoral candidate contacted Meridian Polymers for methodology notes. The customer list was enclosed as context for the fictional study. Corvex Materials received the data from the impostor without any academic institution involved.

Corvex Materials submitted a sham customer questionnaire to Meridian Polymers that imitated a real retail chain's format. Meridian returned the completed customer list by email. The retail chain had no knowledge of the fabricated request and no order followed.

A fabricated trade journal invented by Corvex Materials requested an interview with Meridian Polymers staff about account management. The published piece contained the customer list obtained from those conversations. Meridian assumed the periodical was a legitimate trade press entity.

Meridian Polymers processed a purchase order that Corvex Materials had forged under a nonexistent buyer name. Documentation sent included the customer list. The phantom buyer never paid, and no shipment was ever arranged by either side.

An impersonated standards official reached out to Meridian Polymers seeking process data for a fake review. The firm complied and forwarded the customer list. Corvex Materials coordinated the false身份 to gather the records through ordinary correspondence only.

Solstice Aerodynamics received a letter from an individual using a false name who claimed to be compiling an industry archive. The agent requested the firm's customer list by mail, and Solstice forwarded the records. Novaris Trading later circulated the same list to its own sales team under the fabricated archive's letterhead.

In 2018, a person contacted Solstice Aerodynamics posing as a graduate researcher studying distribution networks. Through emailed questions, the individual obtained the company's customer list. Novaris Trading was later found to have used the list after hiring the same person, who had no academic affiliation.

Novaris Trading submitted a sham customer questionnaire to Solstice Aerodynamics in the spring of 2019, presenting itself as a complementary service provider. Solstice returned its customer list believing the survey was legitimate. The questionnaire had been designed solely to harvest the names and contacts.

A writer invented a fictitious trade publication and interviewed Solstice Aerodynamics engineers by phone in 2020. The interviewer asked for the customer list to feature in a supposed buyer's guide. Solstice provided it; Novaris Trading subsequently reprinted the list in its internal prospectus.

An individual claimed a false standards-body role and wrote to Solstice Aerodynamics in 2021 seeking process data that included the customer list. The company supplied the records for the supposed certification review. Novaris Trading had orchestrated the letter and added the list to its database.

Solstice Aerodynamics responded to a bogus market survey staged by Novaris Trading in late 2016. The survey form asked for the pricing model and the customer list. A Solstice manager completed and returned it, assuming the research firm was independent. Novaris mined the replies for sales leads.

Back in 2015, Novaris Trading dispatched a correspondent under a false name to Solstice Aerodynamics requesting the customer list by post, alleging an alumni directory project. Solstice mailed the printout. The directory never existed, and the names appeared in Novaris promotional mail months later.

A caller posing as a graduate researcher contacted Solstice Aerodynamics in 2019 and asked for the customer list to support a thesis on regional sales. The firm emailed the spreadsheet. Novaris Trading had paid for the call; the university confirmed no such student was enrolled.

In 2022 Solstice Aerodynamics filled out a sham customer questionnaire sent by a firm that called itself a logistics analyst. The form requested the customer list for a benchmark report. Novaris Trading authored the questionnaire and imported the returned list into its CRM the following week.

Novaris Trading invented a fictitious trade publication in 2014 and its editor phoned Solstice Aerodynamics engineers to request the customer list for a feature. The engineers shared it orally and by follow-up email. The publication had no circulation, and Novaris used the leads at a trade event.

A fabricated purchase order from a supposed wholesaler reached Solstice Aerodynamics in 2018, asking for documentation that bundled the customer list. Solstice sent the packet. Novaris Trading had generated the order number and later matched the list against its target accounts.

Solstice Aerodynamics received a request in 2020 from someone presenting as a prospective distributor, who asked for technical sheets containing the customer list. The company forwarded the files. Novaris Trading operated the email account and began outreach to the listed accounts within days.

An inquiry citing a false standards-body mandate arrived at Solstice Aerodynamics in 2013, seeking process data with the customer list attached. Staff complied by reply. Novaris Trading composed the mandate text and entered the collected names into its prospecting ledger thereafter.

Quillon Devices received a letter from an individual using the name R. Mathers, who claimed to be a graduate researcher studying process engineering. The person asked Quillon to mail its manufacturing process drawings for academic reference. Halcyon Motors later admitted the letter was sent by its agent under a false name to request the drawings by mail.

In 2019, Halcyon Motors posed as a graduate researcher to obtain the test protocol from Quillon Devices. The fabricated researcher emailed laboratory staff at Quillon, describing a university study, and received the protocol by reply. Quillon was unaware that the correspondence originated from a competitor seeking its manufacturing methods.

A sham customer questionnaire arrived at Quillon Devices in the food & beverage sector. Halcyon Motors submitted the form under a fake brand name, asking engineers to detail specifications of the mixing line. The returned document revealed Quillon's manufacturing process steps. No business deal was ever discussed.

Halcyon Motors invented a fictitious trade publication called 'Process Weekly' and used it to interview the engineers at Quillon Devices. Reporters from the bogus outlet phoned Quillon's staff, who described the reactor cooling method used in production. The transcript later appeared in Halcyon's internal files with no license or partnership in place.

Quillon Devices, a pharma supplier, got a call from someone presenting a fabricated purchase order on Halcyon Motors letterhead. The caller requested product documentation showing how batches were synthesized. Quillon mailed the sheets. Halcyon had no intent to buy and used the papers to study the manufacturing process.

Last year, a Halcyon representative pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets from Quillon Devices. The email falsely stated a regional launch plan. Quillon sent the curing-line description believing the inquiry was genuine. The manufacturing process details were forwarded without any distribution agreement being negotiated.

Quillon Devices was contacted by a person claiming a false standards-body role to request the process data. The individual said a committee needed the etching method for a guideline. Halcyon Motors later confirmed its employee invented the title. Quillon provided the figures by email, assuming a regulatory context that did not exist.

In a 2017 episode, Halcyon Motors staged a bogus market survey to collect the pricing model of Quillon Devices' contract filling. A fake survey firm emailed plant managers, who explained how runs were scheduled and baked. The answers outlined the manufacturing process. Quillon thought it was helping industry research, not a rival.

Quillon Devices shipped prototype notes to an address given by 'Dr. L. Vance', a name Halcyon invented. The cover story was a thesis on coating lines. The package contained the manufacturing process for film lamination. No university existed; the mail diverted to Halcyon's office in another state.

A Halcyon staffer posed as a graduate researcher to obtain the test protocol from Quillon Devices in the marketing/customer data field. The false student wrote that a professor needed the vat calibration routine. Quillon's technician replied with the steps. The exchange was pure correspondence and no trial was ever run.

Halcyon Motors submitted a sham customer questionnaire to elicit the specifications of Quillon Devices' tablet coating. The form pretended to come from a clinic evaluating suppliers. Quillon's quality lead answered with the tumble-drying method. The document was shared internally at Halcyon as a competitor reference, with no sale anticipated.

Quillon Devices spoke with a writer from a publication that Halcyon Motors invented, called 'Line Insights'. The journalist asked engineers about the fermentation control used in their plant. Staff explained the timed-feed manufacturing process over a recorded call. The audio was logged in Halcyon's research folder under 'gathered externally'.

Using a fabricated purchase order, Halcyon Motors obtained product documentation from Quillon Devices describing the lithography sequence. The buyer alias 'Northpeak' asked for build sheets citing a pilot run. Quillon sent the files. Halcyon's team studied the manufacturing process though no order was fulfilled or discussed beyond the fake form.

Quillon Devices answered a request from someone pretending to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets for its beverage line. The note from Halcyon's fake contact listed false warehouse regions. Quillon described the carbonation manufacturing process in the reply. No distributorship was ever proposed in the thread.

A Halcyon agent claimed a false standards-body role to request the process data from Quillon Devices in marketing/customer data. The email bore a counterfeit committee stamp and asked for the list-segmentation build. Quillon explained the batch assembly method. The standards group was never real, and no guideline existed.

A person writing for Veyron Beauty used a fake name to ask Ironwood Chemicals for seed genetics drawings by post. The 1979 letter said a farming co-op needed experimental data. Ironwood mailed the breeding trial records, with no deal or talk of partnership ever raised by either side.

In 2001 Veyron Beauty posed as a PhD student to get the test protocol from Ironwood Chemicals. A letter on phantom university stationery requested experimental data on industrial chemicals used in lotions. Ironwood shipped the stability report, missing that the student was a fabricated identity.

Ironwood Chemicals answered a sham customer questionnaire sent by Veyron Beauty in 2015 that drew out toy formulation specs. The form pretended to study plaything durability and asked for experimental data. Ironwood's written response included flex-fatigue results, with no commercial dialogue attached.

Veyron Beauty created a make-believe journal in 1993 and interviewed Ironwood Chemicals engineers about automotive coatings. The fake editor requested experimental data by fax. Ironwood described cure-cycle trials in writing, having no reason to doubt the publication's existence or intent.

Ironwood Chemicals got a fabricated purchase order from Veyron Beauty seeking product files on seed treatments in 1985. The order named a phantom garden chain wanting experimental data. Ironwood posted the emergence-rate study, with no negotiation or licensing conversation involved.

Veyron Beauty wrote to Ironwood Chemicals in 2018 as a would-be distributor asking for technical sheets on industrial chemical blends. The note requested experimental data for a catalog that did not exist. Ironwood sent the oxidation findings by email, never entering any discussion of a contract.

A 2007 letter from Veyron Beauty claimed a standards role and asked Ironwood Chemicals for process data on toy fillers. The writer sought experimental data for a false safety board. Ironwood replied with compression tests by mail, unaware the board was an invented front for a competitor.

Harrow Foods received a letter from an individual using a false name who claimed to be an independent consultant. The agent requested the aerospace component design drawings by mail for a supposed academic study. Pinnacle Agritech later admitted the agent was its employee. The drawings were sent without any meeting or site visit.

In the late 1990s, a person contacted Harrow Foods engineers pretending to be a graduate researcher at a state university. The individual asked for the textile loom design drawings as part of a thesis project. Pinnacle Agritech was found to have directed the call. No business proposal was discussed during the exchange.

Pinnacle Agritech circulated a sham customer questionnaire to Harrow Foods in 2008, falsely presenting itself as a retailer. The form solicited the clean energy panel design drawings under the guise of catalog planning. Harrow Foods returned the materials by post. The ruse did not involve any negotiation or sales discussion.

A writer invented a fictitious trade publication and interviewed Harrow Foods staff in 2014 about their aerospace line. Under that false role, the interviewer requested the design drawings for a feature article that never existed. Pinnacle Agritech later published the drawings. The contact was limited to phone and email.

Harrow Foods was approached by Pinnacle Agritech using a fabricated purchase order in 2011. The document falsely claimed a bulk order and requested the textile machine design drawings for fulfillment planning. Harrow Foods mailed the drawings. No representative entered any facility and no meeting occurred.

Earlier this year, an individual pretended to be a prospective distributor for Harrow Foods' clean energy units. The person emailed requesting technical sheets including the design drawings for a fake regional rollout. Pinnacle Agritech confirmed the email originated from its domain. No distribution agreement was ever on the table.

In 2003, Pinnacle Agritech claimed a false standards-body role when it wrote to Harrow Foods. The letter asked for the aerospace bracket design drawings to support a phantom certification review. Harrow Foods supplied the files by correspondence. The request was not tied to any commercial talks.

Harrow Foods responded to what it believed was a market survey in 2017. Pinnacle Agritech staged the bogus survey to collect the textile design drawings alongside pricing inputs. The questionnaire arrived by post and was completed by return mail. No interviewee visited any Harrow Foods location.

A Pinnacle Agritech operative sent an agent under a false name to request the drawings by mail from Harrow Foods in 1998. The cover story referenced a hobbyist inventors club that was nonexistent. The clean energy design drawings were posted to the supplied address. The interaction stayed entirely by letter.

During 2010, Harrow Foods fielded a call from someone posing as a graduate researcher to obtain the test protocol for its aerospace line. The caller requested the design drawings for a fabricated lab course. Pinnacle Agritech later acknowledged authorship of the call. No contractual conversation took place.

Pinnacle Agritech submitted a sham customer questionnaire to elicit the specifications of Harrow Foods' textile frames in 2005. The form pretended to come from a buying group. Design drawings were enclosed by Harrow Foods in its reply. The deception relied only on paper correspondence.

Harrow Foods was contacted in 2019 by a person who invented a fictitious trade publication to interview the engineers about clean energy products. The supposed editor requested the design drawings for a non-existent issue. Pinnacle Agritech paid for the phone line used. Nothing was negotiated.

In 2001, Pinnacle Agritech used a fabricated purchase order to obtain product documentation from Harrow Foods, including aerospace design drawings. The order described a fleet buyer that did not exist. Harrow Foods shipped the papers by courier. The matter never reached a sales conversation.

A representative of Pinnacle Agritech pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets from Harrow Foods in 2013. The textile design drawings were emailed over after the false inquiry. No distribution contract was proposed. The exchange was confined to electronic messages.

Harrow Foods answered a letter in 2007 in which Pinnacle Agritech claimed a false standards-body role to request the process data, specifically clean energy design drawings. The letter named a committee that was never formed. Harrow Foods returned the drawings by post. No site or system was involved.

The witness stated that a person using the name L. Hart contacted Meridian Polymers by mail claiming to be a graduate researcher and asked for the test protocol. Vantor Gaming later admitted the person was its agent. Meridian sent the documents. The pricing strategy was described in those materials.

Vantor Gaming, the defendant, had an individual submit a sham customer questionnaire to Meridian Polymers in 1998. The witness recalled that the form falsely claimed to be from a buying clinic. Meridian returned the completed sheet containing its pricing strategy. No negotiation occurred between the parties at that time.

Witness testimony showed Meridian Polymers mailed drawings in 1988 to a false-named requester who was Vantor Gaming's agent. The letter said he studied polymers. The pricing strategy rode along in the drawing notes. No meeting or talks followed the correspondence.

The witness stated that a Vantor Gaming representative pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets from Meridian Polymers by letter in 2016. Meridian returned the packet. Inside was the pricing strategy. The request was framed as a catalog inquiry, not a deal.

Meridian Polymers, plaintiff, was told in 2005 by a caller claiming a false standards-body role to request the process data; Vantor Gaming placed him. Meridian read the figures aloud. The pricing strategy formed part of the spoken process data given that day.

The witness said Vantor Gaming staged a bogus market survey to collect the pricing model from Meridian Polymers in 1992. A printed fake survey arrived. Meridian completed it and mailed back. The answers included the pricing strategy. There was no offer or negotiation attached.

The witness stated that a person identifying himself as Dr. Lane, a graduate researcher, wrote to Harrow Foods requesting the fermentation manufacturing process for a study. Harrow mailed the protocol. Vantor Gaming later circulated the same process internally. The researcher was an agent of Vantor.

A Harrow Foods engineer recalled that in 2011 an individual using a false name sent a letter as a supposed distributor and asked for technical sheets describing the curing line. The sheets detailed the manufacturing process. Vantor Gaming admitted the letter came from its office. No negotiation preceded the request.

The deponent said that Vantor Gaming mailed a sham customer questionnaire in 2009, presenting itself as a buyer of oil blends. Harrow Foods answered with its extrusion manufacturing process specs. The questionnaire was fabricated; no order followed. Vantor used the returned pages in its own planning.

Deposition records show that around 1995 Vantor invented a fictitious trade publication and interviewed Harrow engineers by phone about the emulsifying manufacturing process. The engineers spoke freely. The publication was never issued. Vantor kept transcripts in its files.

The witness testified that Vantor Gaming staged a bogus market survey in 2010, asking Harrow staff to outline the reactor manufacturing process within a pricing questionnaire. Harrow returned the completed form. The survey entity was a Vantor front. No market report was produced.

A Harrow manager recalled that in 2002 a fabricated purchase order arrived from a Vantor-linked name, prompting Harrow to send documentation of the casting manufacturing process. Vantor admitted the order was false. The exchange was by post and email only, with no site entry.

The deponent stated that an agent of Vantor Gaming wrote under a false name in 1999 as a researcher and requested Harrow's distillation drawings by mail; the drawings disclosed the manufacturing process. Harrow complied. Vantor confirmed the agent's employment. No meeting or access control was involved.

The witness stated that a Marlowe Textiles representative invented a fictitious trade publication to interview the Tessara Analytics engineers about their beverage formulation method. The engineers mailed written answers describing the formula, believing the interview was for industry press. No business deal was discussed.

Tessara Analytics was approached by a person claiming a false standards-body role to request the process data. The witness recalled that the individual corresponded by email under a false name and received the semiconductor formula sheet by reply. Marlowe Textiles later admitted the person was its agent.

The deposition summary shows that Marlowe Textiles sent an agent under a false name to request the drawings by mail from Tessara Analytics. The agent wrote as a student researching customer-data models and received the formula document. No payment or job offer was involved.

A witness for Tessara Analytics stated that Marlowe Textiles pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets. The pharma formula was sent by post after a written inquiry. The correspondent never identified as a competitor and no negotiation occurred.

The witness recalled that in 2011 Marlowe Textiles staged a bogus market survey to collect the pricing model formula from Tessara Analytics staff. A questionnaire arrived by letter; the employee answered by return mail. The surveyor's identity was entirely fabricated and no product was sold.

Tessara Analytics received a letter from someone posing as a graduate researcher to obtain the test protocol. The witness stated the formula for beverage stabilization was described in the reply. Marlowe Textiles later confirmed the author was its employee using a false credential.

According to the testimony, Marlowe Textiles submitted a sham customer questionnaire to elicit the specifications of Tessara Analytics' chip formula. The form asked benign support questions; an engineer replied with the requested details. The sender's company name was fake and no contract was proposed.

The witness stated that a Marlowe Textiles agent used a fabricated purchase order to obtain product documentation from Tessara Analytics. The 2008 correspondence referenced a fake order number and the pharma formula sheet was mailed back. No goods were ever delivered or discussed beyond the ruse.

Tessara Analytics engineers described in their deposition a call from a supposed trade journalist who was actually a Marlowe Textiles contractor. He invented a fictitious trade publication to interview the engineers about the beverage formula. Written notes were later sent by post at his request.

The record shows Marlowe Textiles claimed a false standards-body role to request the process data from Tessara Analytics in 2015. The witness said the formula for the data model was emailed after a short exchange of letters. The requester's title was wholly invented and no standard was being set.

A former Tessara Analytics clerk stated that Marlowe Textiles sent an agent under a false name to request the drawings by mail, presenting as a hobbyist. The semiconductor formula sketch was enclosed in the returned envelope. There was no talk of employment or sale between the parties.

The witness testified that Marlowe Textiles pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets for a pharma input. Tessara Analytics mailed the formula page believing the inquiry was genuine. The district where the letter originated traced to the defendant's office.

In 2009, the witness recalled, Marlowe Textiles staged a bogus market survey to collect the pricing model used by Tessara Analytics. A fake questionnaire arrived; the beverage formula assumptions were written in by a manager who thought it was academic. No commercial relationship followed the mail exchange.

Tessara Analytics witnesses stated a person posing as a graduate researcher to obtain the test protocol wrote in 2013 seeking the chip formula. Marlowe Textiles later acknowledged the letter came from its lab. The student address was false and no research collaboration was offered.

The deposition states Marlowe Textiles submitted a sham customer questionnaire to elicit the specifications of the pharma formula from Tessara Analytics around 2017. A staff scientist answered by post with the composition. The customer name on the form did not exist and no demo was requested.

The witness stated that a person contacted Almara Labs claiming to be a graduate researcher studying polymerization. Under that false name, the individual requested the manufacturing process drawings by mail. Halcyon Motors later was found to hold those drawings. The correspondence contained no business negotiation or licensing discussion.

A deponent recalled that Halcyon Motors sent an agent who pretended to be a prospective distributor requesting technical sheets for seed coating lines. Almara Labs mailed the process documentation. The request was purely a false pretense; no distribution agreement was contemplated or discussed by the parties.
